html:
A stone wall across northern England, begun in 122 CE on the orders of the emperor Hadrian. It ran about 117 km from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth and marked the northern frontier of the Roman Empire in Britain.

Rome had conquered Britain from 43 CE, after Claudius invaded, but never held the far north. Hadrian chose to fix the empire's borders rather than push them out. The wall had small forts every Roman mile, turrets between them, larger forts along its length, and ditches in front and behind. It controlled movement and trade as much as it kept raiders out.

Soldiers from across the empire, from Syria to the Rhine, served here. Writing tablets found at Vindolanda, a fort nearby, show daily life on the frontier: a birthday invitation, requests for socks and beer. Under Antoninus Pius the Romans moved north to the Antonine Wall for some twenty years, then came back. The wall was held until the end of Roman rule around 410. Compare the Great Wall of China.
